To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the adsorption energy (ΔEads) of PXDD@C 60 complexes is strongly correlated to the molecular structure of the adsorbed PXDD.
the QSPR modeling of the adsorption energy of 1,701 halogenated dibenziopdioxins (PXD, X = Br or C1) on C60 fullerens is reported.
the adsorption energy (kcal/mol) for 1, 701 PXDDs on C60 fullerens is predicted with a high accuracy (R2 =0.998).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prediction of the adsorption energies of dibenzo-p- dioxins on the C60 surface, which is of great importance for their potential application as sorbents.
the development of a predictive model for the adsorption of PXDDs on C60, which could be useful in the design of new fullerene sorbents.
the development of an efficient and accurate computational method for the prediction of the sorption ability of halogenated dibenazo-p-dioxins onto fullerene.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the C60 fullerence is not an efficient sorbent of halogenated dibenzi-p-dioxins.
the most toxic congeners are the least adsorbed, but that the least toxic congeners are also the most adsorbed.
the most toxic congeners (i.e., those that are the most likely to bind to the AhR) are the least effective in binding to the fullerene, whereas less toxic congeners are more effective.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the QSPR approach is a powerful tool that allows the prediction of adsorption energies of organic molecules on organic surfaces, which can be used for the design of new materials and/or the optimization of already known sorbent agents.

the sorption ability of C60 fullerene for dibenzo-p- dioxins is influenced by halogenation and that the sorption effectiveness is not necessarily correlated with the environmental risk posed by the dioxin congeners.
the sorption of dibenzo-p- dioxins on C-60 is a function of the halogen substitution pattern.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sorption ability of fullerenes is not only dependent on their large surface area, but also on their chemical structure, and the chemical structure of the pollutant.
the sorption ability of C60 is not influenced by the presence of halogen atoms, and that the sorption of dibenzo-pdioxins is not selective with respect to the presence of halogens.
the C60 fullerence is a promising sorbent for the removal of halogenated dioxin from the environment.
